title: The copyright on "Happy Birthday"
hook: The world's best-known song was treated as private property until 2016.
peek: For decades a music publisher collected fees whenever "Happy Birthday to You" was sung in a film or on TV, earning millions. Then a documentary maker challenged the copyright in court, and a judge found the claim did not hold up.
lede: The tune of "Happy Birthday to You" comes from "Good Morning to All", a song for young children published by two Kentucky sisters, Mildred and Patty Hill, in 1893. More than a century later a music publisher was still charging for its use. Films and TV shows paid fees, or wrote around the song to avoid them.

bullets.text: Patty Hill was a kindergarten teacher, and the original words greeted a class each morning. At some point people began singing new birthday words to the same tune, and the birthday version spread on its own.
A copyright was registered in 1935, and in 1988 the publisher Warner/Chappell bought the company that held it. The song was widely reported to earn around $2 million a year in licensing fees.

The filmmaker Jennifer Nelson, who wanted to use the song in a documentary about it, sued in 2013. In 2015 a federal judge ruled that the publisher had never shown it owned the lyrics, and a settlement in 2016 left the song free to use in the United States.

Many restaurant chains created their own birthday chants for staff to sing at tables. The usual explanation was to avoid any risk of a licensing fee, which is why so many of them sound nothing like the real song.

Shared birthdays turn up more often than people expect, so one office or classroom can need the song twice on the same day. In a group of just 23 people, there is better than an even chance that two share a birthday.
The case is one of several famous fights over who owns a piece of music, alongside the drum break on a 1969 B-side that was copied into thousands of records.
